title: How to Import CoinPoker Hand Histories into PokerTracker 4
excerpt: CoinPoker's export looks close to PokerStars format but isn't — here's exactly why PokerTracker 4 rejects it, and how to fix it in under a minute.
body:
## Why CoinPoker hands don't import cleanly into PokerTracker 4

CoinPoker's hand history export *looks* like the PokerStars-style format PokerTracker 4 expects — close enough to be confusing when the import silently fails or your stats come out wrong. Four differences cause almost every problem:

**The header.** CoinPoker writes `CoinPoker Hand #130114200045: NLH (₮0.01/₮0.02)`. PokerTracker 4's parser is looking for a specific header shape and the full game name, `Hold'em No Limit`, not the `NLH` code.

**The ₮ currency sign.** CoinPoker prices everything in USDT and prints the tether sign, `₮0.02`, with no currency code attached. PokerTracker 4 wants `$0.02` (or the equivalent in whatever currency code it recognizes).

**A "Dealt to" line for every player.** CoinPoker prints `Dealt to <PlayerName>` for the whole table, not just you. PokerTracker 4 only expects to see the hero's hole cards — the extra lines confuse the parser and can cause it to misread the rest of the hand.

**Timezone and stray lines.** CoinPoker timestamps hands in the server's local time (commonly CEST), and adds lines like `Hand was run once` and `Game ended:` that don't exist in the format PokerTracker 4 reads.

None of this is a bug in CoinPoker's export — it's just a different dialect. The fix is a straight text conversion, not a workaround inside PokerTracker 4 itself.

## Converting your hand histories

1. Export your hand history file from CoinPoker as you normally would (`.txt`).
2. Upload it to [PokerHandsConverter](/) — cash games and full sessions both work, and tournament hands are detected automatically.
3. Download the converted file and point PokerTracker 4's importer at it, the same way you'd import any other tracker-ready file.

The header, currency, "Dealt to" lines and timestamps are all rewritten in the process, so the file PokerTracker 4 sees is one it already knows how to read.

## After you import

If PokerTracker 4 throws a pot-size or rake error on a handful of hands, see [Fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors on CoinPoker imports](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import) — it's almost always one specific summary-line format.

Once hands are importing cleanly, the next step is usually [setting up your first HUD](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) so the stats actually show up at the table — and once it's live, it's worth learning [what VPIP, PFR and 3-bet% actually mean](/blog/understanding-vpip-pfr-3bet-hud-stats) before you start making decisions off them.

## Which trackers does this work with?

The same conversion feeds PokerTracker 4, Hold'em Manager 3, Hand2Note and DriveHUD — see the [PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3](/blog/pokertracker-4-vs-holdem-manager-3-coinpoker) comparison if you haven't picked one yet, or [Hand2Note vs PokerTracker 4](/blog/hand2note-vs-pokertracker-4) for a third option.

## If you're still deciding where to play

Tracker compatibility is just one factor in picking a room in the first place — see [how to choose an online poker room](/blog/how-to-choose-an-online-poker-room) for the fuller checklist, including rake and rakeback.

title: CoinPoker vs PokerStars Hand History Format: What's Different
excerpt: A field-by-field breakdown of why CoinPoker's hand history export isn't compatible with PokerStars-style trackers out of the box.
body:
## Two formats that look alike and aren't

If you've only ever played on PokerStars-descended sites, a CoinPoker hand history reads as *almost* familiar — same general shape, same idea of seats and streets and a summary line. The specific fields are different enough that a tracker built for PokerStars-style imports (which is most of them) rejects CoinPoker's export outright, or worse, imports it with wrong numbers.

## Field-by-field differences

**Hand header.** PokerStars-style: `PokerStars Hand #123: Hold'em No Limit ($0.01/$0.02 USD) - 2026/09/09 12:01:21 ET`. CoinPoker: `CoinPoker Hand #130114200045: NLH (₮0.01/₮0.02) 2026/09/09 12:01:21 CEST`. Different hand-id prefix, an abbreviated game code (`NLH` instead of the full name), and the tether sign instead of a dollar sign with a currency code.

**Currency.** CoinPoker denominates cash games in USDT and prints the ₮ symbol throughout — blinds, bets, the summary, everywhere an amount appears. Trackers expecting `$` (or an explicit `USD` code) don't recognize ₮ as a currency at all, so every amount in the hand looks unparseable.

**Hole cards.** CoinPoker's export includes a `Dealt to <name>` line for every player at the table, since the client itself has visibility CoinPoker chooses to log. Trackers expect exactly one `Dealt to` line — yours — and can misparse the hand when they hit extra ones for opponents.

**Timezone.** CoinPoker stamps hands in the server's local time, with no explicit "ET" marker, while PokerStars-style trackers generally expect either a bare local timestamp or an explicit Eastern-time stamp depending on how they're configured. It's a formatting choice, not a data problem — get it wrong and a session can look shifted by a few hours or split into two, without any hand actually being corrupted.

**Fee lines.** Some CoinPoker cash tables add a `Splash Fee` on top of rake in the summary line — a fee type PokerStars-style parsers have no concept of. Left as-is, it breaks rake parsing on the hand entirely; see [CoinPoker rake and Splash Fee explained](/blog/coinpoker-rake-splash-fee-explained) for exactly how.

**Extra bookkeeping lines.** `Hand was run once`, `Game ended:` and similar lines are informational text CoinPoker adds that don't correspond to anything in the PokerStars-style format, and get treated as noise.

## Why this matters beyond "it won't import"

Even when a tracker *does* manage to import a raw CoinPoker file, misreading the currency sign or an extra "Dealt to" line can silently produce wrong pot sizes, wrong win-rates, or a HUD that shows stats for the wrong player. A hand that imports without an error isn't the same as a hand that imported *correctly* — and a wrong win-rate is worse than no win-rate, since it's easy to trust a number that looks plausible.

## The practical fix

Rather than trying to reconfigure a tracker's parser (most don't expose that), convert the file first: [see the full CoinPoker → PokerTracker 4 walkthrough](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4).

title: PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3 for CoinPoker: Which Should You Use?
excerpt: Both trackers work fine with CoinPoker hands once converted — here's what actually differs between them so you can pick one.
body:
## Same job, different tools

PokerTracker 4 and Hold'em Manager 3 both do the same core job — import hand histories, compute stats, and feed a HUD at the table — and both work fine with CoinPoker hands once they're converted to a format either one recognizes. The choice between them mostly comes down to interface preference and which one your study group or coaching material already uses, not raw capability.

## PokerTracker 4

PokerTracker 4 has been around the longest of the two, and it shows in the depth of its filtering and reporting — if you like slicing your database by very specific situations (3-bet pots from the blinds, specific stack-depth ranges, and so on), PT4's report builder is built for exactly that. The HUD is fully customizable panel by panel, which is powerful but has a steeper setup curve the first time — see [setting up your first HUD in PokerTracker 4](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) if you're starting from scratch.

## Hold'em Manager 3

Hold'em Manager 3 leans more modern in its interface, with a replayer and stats views that are generally considered a bit more approachable out of the box. It covers the same core stat set as PT4 and is a common choice for players who want less configuration before they can start reviewing sessions.

## What actually matters for CoinPoker players specifically

Neither tracker understands CoinPoker's raw export — the ₮ currency sign, the abbreviated `NLH` header, and the extra `Dealt to` lines trip up both parsers the same way. [PokerHandsConverter](/) converts to a format both trackers read correctly, so the choice between PT4 and HM3 doesn't depend on which one "supports" CoinPoker — they both do, once the file is converted.

## If you're not sure yet

A reasonable default: if you already use one for other sites, keep using it — switching trackers mid-database is more friction than it's worth for most players. If you're starting from zero, try the free/trial version of each on a small batch of converted hands and see which interface you reach for without thinking. There's a third common option worth knowing about too — see [Hand2Note vs PokerTracker 4](/blog/hand2note-vs-pokertracker-4) if fast visual range analysis appeals more than deep custom reporting. Whichever you pick, the stats it shows you are only as useful as your sample size — see [how many hands you need before your stats are reliable](/blog/sample-size-reliable-poker-stats) before you draw conclusions from a new database.

title: How to Set Up Your First HUD for CoinPoker in PokerTracker 4
excerpt: A HUD only shows what's in your database. Here's how to get from zero hands imported to a working, readable HUD at the table.
body:
## Why the HUD doesn't "just appear"

A HUD (heads-up display) overlays live stats — VPIP, PFR, 3-bet%, and whatever else you configure — directly on the table while you play. It's driven entirely by hands already sitting in your tracker's database, so if it isn't showing anything, the usual cause is one of two things: no hands have been imported yet, or the HUD hasn't been pointed at the right site/table type.

## Before you touch HUD settings

Make sure your CoinPoker hands are actually importing first. If PokerTracker 4 is throwing errors on import, the HUD has nothing to draw from — see [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) and, if a subset of hands specifically error out, [fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import).

## Setting up a basic HUD

1. **Import a session first.** You need at least a few dozen hands in the database before stats are meaningful — a brand-new HUD showing "0 hands" everywhere isn't broken, it just has nothing to show yet.
2. **Pick a HUD profile.** PokerTracker 4 ships default profiles (a simple one, a more detailed one) — start with a simple profile rather than building a custom panel layout from scratch on day one.
3. **Choose your stat panels.** The standard starting set most players settle on is VPIP, PFR, 3-bet%, and a hand count (so you know how much to trust the numbers yet) — see [understanding VPIP, PFR and 3-bet%](/blog/understanding-vpip-pfr-3bet-hud-stats) if those terms aren't familiar yet.
4. **Match it to the table.** HUD profiles can be table-size specific (6-max vs full ring) and game-type specific (cash vs tournament) — population tendencies shift enough between formats that a HUD tuned for one won't read cleanly on the other. See [6-max vs full ring cash games](/blog/6max-vs-full-ring-cash-games) for what actually changes.
5. **Sit down and confirm it's live.** Open a table (or the replayer) and check the panel renders and updates — small sample sizes will make the numbers jump around a lot at first, which is expected, not a sign anything's wrong.

## Reading small samples correctly

Early on, a HUD stat built on 20 hands can look extreme — a 45% VPIP that means almost nothing yet. See [how many hands you need before your stats are reliable](/blog/sample-size-reliable-poker-stats) for roughly how large a sample has to get before different stats start meaning something.

## Once it's working

If you switch between PokerTracker 4 and Hold'em Manager 3, or haven't picked yet, the HUD setup differs in interface but not in the underlying idea — see [PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3 for CoinPoker](/blog/pokertracker-4-vs-holdem-manager-3-coinpoker) for how they compare.

title: Fixing "Invalid Pot Size" Errors When Importing CoinPoker Hands
excerpt: Almost every 'Invalid Pot Size' error on a CoinPoker import traces back to one specific summary-line format. Here's how to fix it.
body:
## The single most common CoinPoker import error

If PokerTracker 4 rejects a CoinPoker hand with something like *"Invalid pot size"* — and it's happening on a large share of your hands, not just one or two — there's a specific, well-understood cause: a newer CoinPoker summary-line format that includes a **Splash Fee** alongside the rake.

## What's actually in the file

A normal CoinPoker summary line looks like:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18
```

Some cash tables now add a Splash Fee on top:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18 | Splash Fee ₮0.02
```

PokerTracker 4 has no concept of a "Splash Fee" — and its presence in the line doesn't just get ignored, it stops PT4 from reading the `Rake` figure at all. PT4 then computes rake as `0`, checks that against the pot it calculated independently from the betting action, finds a mismatch, and rejects the hand as an invalid pot.

## Why it looks stake-specific (but isn't)

Because the Splash Fee shows up more often on certain tables, this can look like a stakes-specific bug at first — "my NL10 hands are fine but NL2 keeps failing." It isn't tied to a stake; it's tied to whichever tables happen to charge that fee. The fix has to apply uniformly, regardless of stake, or you'll just see the same failure resurface on a different table later. See [CoinPoker rake and Splash Fee explained](/blog/coinpoker-rake-splash-fee-explained) for how the fee affects your tracked stats beyond just this import error.

## The fix

[PokerHandsConverter](/) detects the Splash Fee pattern and folds it into the rake figure PokerTracker 4 already understands, so the line above becomes:

```
Total pot $3.67 | Rake $0.20
```

That's the rake PT4's own independent calculation expects — pot equals collected amounts plus rake, balanced, no mismatch, no rejected hand. If you're seeing this error on a file today, re-running it through the converter resolves it without touching anything in PokerTracker 4 itself.

## If you're still seeing pot-size errors after converting

A few other things produce a similar-looking error and are worth ruling out:

- **Run-it-twice boards.** These get flagged as warnings during conversion rather than guessed at silently — check your conversion history for a warning on the specific hand.
- **A genuinely corrupted export.** Rare, but if CoinPoker's own export was truncated mid-file, no converter can reconstruct the missing data.

For the broader list of formatting differences between CoinPoker and PokerStars-style hands (of which Splash Fee is one), see [CoinPoker vs PokerStars hand history format](/blog/coinpoker-vs-pokerstars-hand-history-format).

meta_description: Why PokerTracker 4 rejects CoinPoker hands with an "Invalid Pot Size" error, and how the Splash Fee summary line format causes it.

title: CoinPoker Rake and Splash Fee Explained: How They Affect Your Tracked Stats
excerpt: A newer CoinPoker fee type breaks rake parsing in every major tracker if left unconverted. Here's what it is and how it's handled.
body:
## Rake is old news. Splash Fee is newer, and less understood.

Every poker site takes rake — that part isn't CoinPoker-specific. What trips people up is a newer line item some CoinPoker cash tables add on top of rake: a **Splash Fee**. It's a separate charge, printed separately in the hand summary, and — critically — most PokerStars-style trackers have no idea what to do with it.

## How it shows up in the hand history

A standard summary line:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18
```

With a Splash Fee added:

```
Total pot ₮3.67 | Rake ₮0.18 | Splash Fee ₮0.02
```

The pot total already accounts for both the rake and the Splash Fee — CoinPoker isn't hiding anything, it's just reporting two separate deductions instead of one.

## Why it breaks tracker imports

PokerTracker 4, Hold'em Manager 3 and Hand2Note are all built to expect a summary line that ends after the rake figure. When a Splash Fee is appended, the tracker's parser doesn't recognize the trailing text — and rather than ignoring it gracefully, it typically stops reading the rake figure at all, computes rake as `0`, and then rejects the hand because the pot it calculates from the betting action doesn't match the (now wrong) rake-adjusted total. See [fixing "Invalid Pot Size" errors](/blog/fix-invalid-pot-size-error-coinpoker-import) for the exact mechanics.

## How it affects your tracked stats if left unconverted

Beyond the outright import failures, a Splash Fee that isn't accounted for correctly can distort:

- **Total rake paid** — understated, since the tracker never saw the fee at all.
- **Big-blinds-won-per-100** and similar rate stats — thrown off on any hand where the pot mismatch caused the whole hand to be skipped rather than just misread.
- **Session profit** — skipped hands simply don't count toward the session, which can make a losing session look smaller (or a winning one look bigger) than it actually was.

## The fix

[PokerHandsConverter](/) folds the Splash Fee into the rake figure automatically during conversion, so the tracker sees one number it already understands — `Rake $0.20` instead of `Rake $0.18 | Splash Fee $0.02` — and the pot balances correctly. This applies uniformly across every stake, since the fee isn't tied to any one table type.

## Related reading

For the rest of the formatting gap between CoinPoker and PokerStars-style hand histories — currency signs, headers, timezone — see [CoinPoker vs PokerStars hand history format](/blog/coinpoker-vs-pokerstars-hand-history-format), or start from [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) if you're converting your first file.

title: Understanding VPIP, PFR and 3-Bet%: A Beginner's Guide to HUD Stats
excerpt: What your HUD is actually measuring, and how three numbers — VPIP, PFR and 3-bet% — sketch a player's whole preflop style at a glance.
body:
## What a HUD is actually showing you

A HUD reduces a player's entire history at the table down to a handful of percentages. The three you'll see on almost every default profile — VPIP, PFR and 3-bet% — aren't arbitrary; together they sketch how loose, how aggressive, and how willing to apply pressure preflop a player is, before you've seen a single one of their hands live.

## VPIP: how often money goes in voluntarily

VPIP (Voluntarily Put money In Pot) counts any hand where a player calls or raises preflop — it excludes the blinds when nobody's acted on them yet, since posting a blind isn't a choice. A player who plays 45% of hands is playing very loose; one at 15% is playing very tight. There's no single "correct" number — it depends on position, stakes, and the player's overall strategy — but it's the fastest read on how wide someone's starting range is.

## PFR: how often they raise first

PFR (PreFlop Raise) counts only hands where a player raises before the flop — a subset of VPIP, since you can't raise without voluntarily putting money in. Comparing the two tells you more than either alone.

## The VPIP/PFR gap

A player with VPIP 24% and PFR 22% is playing almost everything aggressively — raising nearly every hand they enter, rarely just calling. A player with VPIP 40% and PFR 10% is doing the opposite: entering a lot of pots passively, calling far more than raising. That gap is often a better read on a player's general style than either number alone, and it's usually the first thing experienced players glance at on an unfamiliar HUD.

## 3-bet%: aggression a level deeper

3-bet% measures how often a player re-raises a raise. It's a smaller sample by nature — it only counts hands where someone else already raised — so it takes longer to stabilize than VPIP or PFR. A high 3-bet% generally signals a player who applies preflop pressure rather than just calling raises; a very low one often signals a passive, calling-heavy style even if their VPIP looks otherwise normal.

## Numbers alone don't tell you the whole story

These stats describe *how often*, not *how well*. A 22/20 player can be a strong, disciplined regular or a straightforward, exploitable one — the HUD tells you the shape of their range, not the quality of their decisions inside it. Read them as a starting point for a read, not a verdict.

## Before you trust any of it

None of these numbers mean much on a small sample — see [how many hands you need before your stats are reliable](/blog/sample-size-reliable-poker-stats) for roughly where VPIP, PFR and 3-bet% actually start to stabilize. And if you haven't set a HUD up yet, [setting up your first HUD in PokerTracker 4](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) covers the basics.
meta_title: Understanding VPIP, PFR and 3-Bet%: A HUD Stats Guide
meta_description: A plain-language guide to VPIP, PFR and 3-bet% — what each HUD stat measures, how to read the gap between them, and what they don't tell you.

title: How Many Hands Do You Need Before Your Poker Stats Are Reliable?
excerpt: A 50-hand upswing or downswing tells you almost nothing. Here's roughly how large a sample has to get before your stats mean something.
body:
## Why a 50-hand upswing (or downswing) tells you nothing

Poker variance is brutal, and it's most deceptive at small sample sizes. A player with a genuinely solid long-run win rate can lose money over their first few hundred hands; a player making real mistakes can be up money over the same stretch. Neither outcome tells you much about the underlying strategy — the noise is simply larger than the signal until the sample gets big.

## Different stats stabilize at different speeds

Not every number needs the same sample size to mean something:

**VPIP and PFR** stabilize relatively fast — a few hundred hands starts giving a rough picture, and by a thousand or so they're fairly representative of a player's general tendencies.

**3-bet%** takes longer, since it only updates on hands where someone else has already raised — a much smaller subset of total hands played. Treat a 3-bet% built on a few hundred hands as a loose guess, not a fact.

**Win rate (bb/100)** is the slowest of all by a wide margin. It's common for a legitimately winning player's win rate to swing from strongly negative to strongly positive and back multiple times across their first several thousand hands purely from variance, with no actual change in how they're playing. Tens of thousands of hands is a more realistic minimum before a win-rate number is worth much confidence — and even then, it comes with a wide margin of error.

## What this means in practice

- **Don't overhaul your strategy off a bad week.** A losing stretch over a few sessions is well within normal variance for even a strong long-run winner.
- **Don't get overconfident off a good week either** — the same variance cuts both directions.
- **Track over months, not sessions.** A single day's graph is close to meaningless on its own; a rolling view across weeks starts to say something.
- **Watch the hand count next to a stat, not just the stat.** A HUD showing "22% VPIP (14 hands)" and "22% VPIP (2,200 hands)" are not equally trustworthy numbers, even though they display the same.

## Where this connects to bankroll

Because win rate takes so long to stabilize, you can't rely on your actual results yet to tell you whether your bankroll is appropriately sized for the game you're playing — see [bankroll management for online cash game players](/blog/bankroll-management-online-cash-games) for a sizing approach that doesn't depend on already knowing your true win rate.

## Reading your HUD with this in mind

If VPIP, PFR and 3-bet% aren't fully familiar yet, [understanding VPIP, PFR and 3-bet%](/blog/understanding-vpip-pfr-3bet-hud-stats) covers what each one actually measures before you start trying to read a small sample of them.
meta_title: How Many Hands for Reliable Poker Stats? Sample Size Guide
meta_description: Why poker variance makes small samples misleading, and roughly how many hands VPIP, PFR, 3-bet% and win rate each need to stabilize.

title: Bankroll Management for Online Cash Game Players
excerpt: A practical, buy-in-based framework for sizing your bankroll, taking shots at higher stakes, and knowing when to move back down.
body:
## Why bankroll management matters more online than live

Online, you can play multiple tables at once, move up and down in stakes in seconds, and rack up a statistically meaningful sample of hands in a single sitting. That's an advantage for improving quickly — and a real risk for going broke quickly if your bankroll isn't sized for the swings that come with it.

## Think in buy-ins, not dollars

The number that matters isn't your bankroll in dollars — it's how many buy-ins deep it is for the stake you're playing. $500 is a healthy cushion at one stake and reckless at another. Reasoning in buy-ins keeps the same rule applicable as you move up or down.

## Rough starting guidelines

For online No-Limit Hold'em cash games, a commonly cited range is **20–40 buy-ins** for a full stake, with the lower end fitting a tighter, lower-variance style and the higher end fitting a looser, more aggressive one (or someone who multi-tables heavily, which increases variance per hour even if it doesn't change variance per hand). These are starting points, not rules carved in stone — your own risk tolerance and how bad a losing stretch you can emotionally absorb without playing worse matter just as much as the math.

Tournaments generally call for a deeper bankroll in buy-ins than cash, since a single tournament's outcome is far more binary (min-cash or bust, roughly) — 50-100+ buy-ins is a common range for regular tournament grinders, wider than cash for exactly that reason.

## Shot-taking and moving down

Bankroll management isn't only about avoiding going broke — it's a framework for two specific decisions:

**Taking a shot at a higher stake** — usually justified once your bankroll comfortably clears the buy-in threshold for that stake, not the moment you technically have enough for one or two buy-ins.

**Moving back down** — the harder discipline. If a downswing eats into your bankroll enough that you're now under-rolled for your current stake, moving down isn't an admission of failure, it's the same math working in the other direction.

## Why this connects to your tracked stats

Your actual win rate takes a long time to stabilize — see [how many hands you need before your stats are reliable](/blog/sample-size-reliable-poker-stats) — which means you generally can't lean on "my real win rate is X" to justify a bankroll size early on. Sizing conservatively while your sample builds is the safer default. And since variance itself differs by game format, see [6-max vs full ring cash games](/blog/6max-vs-full-ring-cash-games) for how the swings compare between the two.

## Getting the numbers right in the first place

None of this works if the hands feeding your tracker's win-rate and profit numbers aren't accurate. If you play on CoinPoker, [converting hands before importing them](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) is what keeps those numbers trustworthy in the first place.

title: 6-Max vs Full Ring Cash Games: What Actually Changes
excerpt: Three or four fewer players changes ranges, HUD baselines, variance and postflop dynamics. Here's what's actually different between the two formats.
body:
## The structural difference

6-max tables seat up to six players; full ring seats up to nine or ten. That single difference — three or four fewer players — cascades into almost everything else that changes between the two formats.

## Ranges get wider

With fewer players to act behind you, hands that are unplayable in early position at a full ring table become reasonable opens in 6-max — there's simply less chance someone behind you wakes up with a monster. Preflop ranges widen across the board, most noticeably from the earlier betting positions, which barely exist in the same way at a 6-max table.

## "Normal" HUD numbers shift

Because ranges are structurally wider, a VPIP that would look loose at a full ring table can be completely standard at 6-max — see [understanding VPIP, PFR and 3-bet%](/blog/understanding-vpip-pfr-3bet-hud-stats) if those stats aren't familiar yet. This is exactly why HUD profiles are usually set up per table size: reading a 6-max-calibrated read onto a full ring table (or the reverse) will systematically mislead you about who's playing loose or tight.

## More hands per hour, faster variance

Fewer players means more hands dealt per hour at 6-max, all else equal — more hands means faster sample accumulation, which is good for statistical confidence, but it also means variance compounds faster in real time. A losing stretch that would take a week to unfold at full ring can happen in a couple of sessions at 6-max. See [bankroll management for online cash game players](/blog/bankroll-management-online-cash-games) for how that affects buy-in sizing.

## Postflop dynamics change too

More multiway pots are typical at full ring, since more players are seeing flops with wider effective ranges behind them; 6-max skews toward more heads-up and three-way pots. Multiway pots reward different postflop decisions — value bets that are fine heads-up can be thin multiway, and bluffs that work against one opponent often don't against two or three.

## Which should you play?

Neither format is objectively better — it's a genuine preference between faster-paced, wider-range 6-max play and the more multiway, position-sensitive game at full ring. Many players settle into one as their primary format simply because switching means re-calibrating what "normal" looks like on their HUD and in their own head, which takes real reps either way. If you play both, keep separate HUD profiles for each rather than one blended view — see [setting up your first HUD](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) if you haven't split yours out yet.
meta_title: 6-Max vs Full Ring Cash Games: Key Differences
meta_description: How 6-max and full ring cash games differ in ranges, normal HUD stat baselines, variance and postflop dynamics — and how to pick between them.

title: What Is Rake in Online Poker (and How It Affects Your Win Rate)
excerpt: Every poker room takes a cut of the game. Here's how rake is actually structured, why it matters more than a few cents a hand suggests, and how to get some of it back.
body:
## Rake, in one sentence

Rake is the fee a poker room takes out of the game for hosting it — the house's cut, taken either from cash pots or as a tournament entry fee on top of the prize pool. It's not unique to any one site; every real-money poker room charges it in some form. What varies a lot is how it's structured, and how much it actually costs you over time.

## How cash game rake is usually structured

Most online cash games use **percentage rake**, taken out of the pot at showdown (or when the pot is won), up to a **cap** — a maximum rake amount regardless of pot size. A common shape is something like 5% up to a cap that scales with stakes and table size. Some rooms instead use **time-based rake**, charging players a flat fee per half-hour seated rather than a cut of each pot — less common online than live, but it exists.

## Tournament rake (the fee)

In tournaments, rake shows up as the "fee" portion of a buy-in — a $10+1 tournament has a $1 fee on top of the $10 that goes to the prize pool. It's usually a fixed percentage of the buy-in, commonly somewhere around 10%, though this varies by site and tournament size.

## Why rake matters more than a few cents a hand suggests

Rake is small on any single hand, but it compounds relentlessly across thousands of hands a serious player sees. At low stakes especially, rake can be a significant fraction of the edge a skilled player has over the field — which is exactly why "rake-adjusted win rate" is a more honest number than raw win rate when comparing your results across different games, stakes, or sites with different rake structures.

## Rake isn't always just "rake"

Some rooms add extra fee line items beyond the standard rake — CoinPoker's Splash Fee is one example, a separate charge on top of rake that shows up on certain cash tables. See [CoinPoker rake and Splash Fee explained](/blog/coinpoker-rake-splash-fee-explained) for how that specific fee is structured and how it can trip up tracking software that isn't expecting it.

## Getting some of it back

Rake isn't necessarily a fixed cost you just absorb — many rooms return a portion of it to players through rakeback or a VIP/rewards program. See [what rakeback is and how it affects your bankroll](/blog/rakeback-and-your-bankroll) for how that works and why it matters more the more volume you play.

## Rake structure is a real factor in picking a room

Because rake compounds so heavily over volume, it's worth weighing alongside traffic, software and rakeback when you're deciding where to actually play — see [how to choose an online poker room](/blog/how-to-choose-an-online-poker-room) for the full checklist.
meta_title: What Is Rake in Online Poker? A Plain-Language Guide
meta_description: How online poker rake actually works — percentage rake, caps, tournament fees — and why it matters more to your win rate than it first appears.

title: What Is Rakeback and How It Affects Your Bankroll
excerpt: Rakeback quietly turns a small loser into a small winner for high-volume players. Here's how it's structured and how to actually factor it into your results.
body:
## What rakeback actually is

Rakeback is a portion of the rake you generate handed back to you — either as a direct cash percentage, or indirectly through a VIP/loyalty program that converts your rake contribution into cashback, bonuses, or tournament tickets. Either way, the effect is the same: it lowers your *effective* rake below the *posted* rake.

## The two common structures

**Flat-rate rakeback** returns a fixed percentage of the rake you pay — straightforward to calculate, and the same regardless of how much you play in a given week or month.

**Tiered VIP programs** return more as your volume increases, often through a points system where points convert to cash, bonuses, or other rewards at increasing rates the higher your tier. These can be worth significantly more than a flat rate for high-volume players, but are harder to estimate in advance since the effective rate depends on how much you play and how long you stay at a given tier.

## Why it matters more than it looks like on paper

A few percentage points of rakeback sounds minor until you run the math over real volume. For a high-volume grinder, rakeback can be the difference between a marginally winning and a comfortably winning month — in some cases it single-handedly turns a small loser into a small winner. It's one of the few levers in poker that adds directly to your bottom line without requiring you to play any better.

## Building it into your actual numbers

Rakeback should factor into how you read your own results, not sit separately from them. If your tracker shows a small loss in raw win rate but you're getting meaningful rakeback back, your *true* result — the number that should actually inform decisions like moving up in stakes — is the combination of the two, not the tracker number alone.

## Where this fits with bankroll management

Rakeback effectively raises your win rate (or shrinks your loss rate) without changing your variance — which makes it a genuine, if modest, edge in the bankroll math. See [bankroll management for online cash game players](/blog/bankroll-management-online-cash-games) for how buy-in sizing works, and factor your real rakeback rate in rather than ignoring it.

## Rakeback and rake are two sides of one number

If you're not sure how the rake you're getting cashback on is even structured in the first place, [what rake is and how it affects your win rate](/blog/what-is-rake-in-online-poker) covers the basics — cash game rake, tournament fees, and how rake compounds over volume.
meta_title: What Is Rakeback? How It Affects Your Bankroll
meta_description: How rakeback and VIP programs work, why they matter more for high-volume players, and how to factor real rakeback into your tracked win rate.

title: How to Choose an Online Poker Room: What Actually Matters
excerpt: Game selection, rake, rakeback and software compatibility all affect your win rate before you've played a hand. Here's what's actually worth checking.
body:
## The decision matters more than it seems

Which room you play on affects your win rate before you've played a single hand — through rake, game selection, and software compatibility. It's worth a genuine look rather than defaulting to whichever site a friend mentioned.

## Game selection and traffic

A room's *player pool* determines how soft or tough your games actually are, independent of your own skill. More traffic generally means more tables running at your preferred stake and format, less time spent waiting for a seat, and — often more importantly — a wider mix of recreational players rather than a pool dominated by regulars grinding the same stakes you are.

## Rake structure

Rake eats into your win rate on every single pot, so it's worth understanding a room's specific structure — the percentage, the cap, and whether it scales sensibly with stakes — before committing serious volume there. See [what rake is and how it actually affects your win rate](/blog/what-is-rake-in-online-poker) for what to actually look at.

## Rakeback and promotions

A room with slightly higher posted rake but a strong rakeback or VIP program can net out better than a lower-rake room with nothing back, especially for higher-volume players. See [what rakeback is and how it affects your bankroll](/blog/rakeback-and-your-bankroll) for how to actually compare offers on equal footing rather than by headline percentage alone.

## Software and tracker compatibility

If you use a HUD or track your results — and if you're reading this, you probably do or should — check whether the room's hand history format is one your tracker reads natively. Some rooms export in a PokerStars-style format trackers already understand out of the box; others, like CoinPoker, use their own format that needs converting first. That's not a reason to avoid a room, just something to plan for — see [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) if that's the room you've landed on.

## Table formats and stakes offered

Check that the room actually spreads the format you want to play at meaningful volume — some rooms are deep at 6-max cash but thin on full ring, or strong on tournaments but light on cash traffic outside peak hours. See [6-max vs full ring cash games](/blog/6max-vs-full-ring-cash-games) if you haven't settled on a primary format yet.

## Security and reputation

Basic diligence still applies: how long the room has operated, how withdrawals are handled, and general reputation among other players are worth a quick check before depositing anything meaningful — the same due diligence you'd apply to any platform holding your money.
meta_title: How to Choose an Online Poker Room: A Practical Checklist
meta_description: What actually matters when picking an online poker room — game selection, rake structure, rakeback, tracker compatibility, and table formats.

title: Hand2Note vs PokerTracker 4: Which Tracker Should You Use?
excerpt: Deep custom reporting or fast visual range analysis — here's how Hand2Note and PokerTracker 4 actually differ, and how to tell which fits your study style.
body:
## Two different philosophies

PokerTracker 4 and Hand2Note both track hands, compute stats, and run a HUD — but they're built around genuinely different ideas of how a player studies. PT4 leans into deep, customizable reporting; Hand2Note leans into fast, visual range and population analysis. Neither is strictly better — they suit different study habits.

## PokerTracker 4: depth and customization

PT4's strength is how far you can slice your database — filtering by very specific spots (3-bet pots from the blinds, particular stack depths, particular positions) and building custom reports around exactly what you're studying. The HUD is fully configurable panel by panel. The tradeoff is a steeper setup curve, especially the first time — see [setting up your first HUD in PokerTracker 4](/blog/setup-hud-coinpoker-pokertracker-4) if you're starting from scratch.

## Hand2Note: visual, range-first analysis

Hand2Note is built around heatmaps and range charts rather than tables of numbers — you see a player's tendencies laid out visually across a 13x13 grid rather than reading a percentage and inferring the range yourself. For players who think in ranges first, this can be a faster way to build reads, both on opponents and on your own play. Its HUD follows the same visual philosophy.

## Population stats and pool-wide tendencies

Both tools let you study population-wide tendencies rather than just individual opponents, useful for exploiting general pool leaks rather than only specific players you've faced before — Hand2Note in particular is often chosen specifically for how accessible this population-level view is.

## Which one fits your study style

If you like building custom reports and drilling into very specific numeric filters, PT4's depth is hard to beat. If you think in ranges and want to *see* a population's tendencies rather than read them off a stat line, Hand2Note's approach tends to click faster. Neither requires you to have picked already — most players form an opinion within a few sessions of trying either on a real database.

## Getting CoinPoker hands into either one

Both expect a PokerStars-style hand history, and neither reads CoinPoker's raw export correctly out of the box — the same conversion feeds both trackers cleanly. See [importing CoinPoker hands into PokerTracker 4](/blog/import-coinpoker-hands-into-pokertracker-4) for the full walkthrough; the conversion itself doesn't change based on which tracker you're importing into.

## Weighing a third option

If you're comparing trackers from scratch, [PokerTracker 4 vs Hold'em Manager 3](/blog/pokertracker-4-vs-holdem-manager-3-coinpoker) covers the other common pairing — between the three, most players land on whichever interface felt least like work within the first hour of using it.
meta_description: Comparing Hand2Note and PokerTracker 4 — custom reporting depth vs visual range and population analysis — to help you pick a poker tracker.
